chapter: From Pittsburgh to Maxine Sullivan: management and style
title: Local talent unappreciated at home and her in-and-out career
summary: Pittsburgh musicians went unrecognized; she's been lucky in dropping in and out, and young people discover swing.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: I mean, I left a lot of good musicians in Pittsburgh when I left and you'll probably never hear them on recordings or on the air or what have you. You just have to be there because every where you go there's a local music clique and they have some good music. You have to get around to just see it all. Thank goodness for the opportunity to travel. I run into a lot of good musicians in my travels these days that have been around for years that I never heard of and never will hear of on record.

Maybe there should be some system that brings people to New York for six months and makes them stars and then they can go back home again. People in the home town would appreciate them a bit more, you know.
I'm not saying the people in

the home town don't appreciate them. Sometimes you go to these towns and you hear the musicians and if you're from out of town and you dare to bring out your horn, I mean, they'll play rings around you. So, I don't know, now that everybody is traveling more and should travel more, that they should get around to hear other music, really, because everybody isn't on record, everybody isn't on the radio and it's worse now.

I mean, this seems to be the case especially in jazz singers. I don't know, I suppose somebody like Helen Merrill, you know, it seems to me, I haven't studied her career very carefully but it seems to me she made a whole bunch of records in the 1950s and dropped out of sight for a long long time. And then maybe, I think in the '60s she recorded with Teddy Wilson and then dropped out again, you know. And that happens time and time again with people.
It does.
And it has happened in your case, in and out.
Sure. Well, I've been lucky because you know, let's face it, after all these years,

you know, something is suppose to happen and I've dropped in and out. I've been lucky in view of the fact that I'm working with good musicians. Now, when I say good musicians I mean musicians that are sort of swing oriented. I don't think I could make it with some of the modern musicians, things like that. And I'm just lucky and I get invited to appear where these musicians are. I still think there are a handful of musicians that play and sound, and have style they had in the thirties, and they are not going to get away from it. There are these distinctions between the type of music like when you say jazz, rock, swing, modern, or whatever, there are differences. I'm stuck in the time zone, you know.

You know, I'm not so sure about that. I mean, when I think of those Ellis Larkins records you made, you can pull those out and there's a timeless quality to those. It's good songs,,impeccably performed, and the accompaniment is terrific...

Well what's happening right now is the fact that a lot of young people are hearing this music for the first time and they are liking it, which is to our advantage. I run into a lot of young people who, so far as I'm concerned, there's been at
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

least two generations of young people who weren't exposed to the Swing era and certainly they weren't exposed to music before the Swing era. And they are hearing this music for the first time. Thank goodness there is a revival, interest in these sounds. I don't think it would have occurred except that certain people are intent upon picking up so to speak with Swing.
Another thing is simply being in this New York area where there's a needier environment. What I mean is a selection of FM radio stations to listen to.
Yeah.
And so there's opportunity for people to be playing and reviving all kinds of music.

Yes there is. I noticed that when I go out of town, so I was down in Wilmington, North Carolina and the North Carolina Jazz Society out there and the first jazz festival, and the patrons and the audience was saying they don't hear that kind of music because in some parts of the Country the Nashville sound is very popular so that's all they get. But that's definitely a type of music that is so territorial, so
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

to speak, you know, you will find areas where that kind of music is prevalent. This does not come under the heading of what's popular in popular music. It's not rock music, it's good. I like country music. It certainly, that is the closest thing to jazz as you're ever going to get because the beat is there. And in fact I imagine a lot of early jazz was influenced by country music. And so country music is here to stay. You don't hear much of that. But I notice lately there are some stations that have been playing a little bit more of country music and as you said, because we do have the different stations and we have a lot of persons now who are interested in swing and jazz.
On the college radio stations.

Yeah, on the college radio stations. These are young people who are discovering swing because a lot of the music has been taken into the colleges and they have a definite interest. And it has to do with, alright so what's American music, number one. And number two, it could be that they are, and I hate to say this, but that they are fed up with this what is considered rock now. It gets to be infantile.

And after you get past a certain age you don't want to hear that. So it makes us feel good, those of us who are still around.
